options.a: Turn the resident toward you by pulling the far arm and shoulder
options.b: Use draw sheets/assistance and keep the spine in alignment
options.c: Raise the head of the bed fully before rolling the resident
options.d: Turn the resident alone quickly to reduce time spent exposed

distractorExplanations.a: Pulling on the arm and shoulder can dislocate joints and twists the spine; a draw sheet keeps the body aligned.
distractorExplanations.c: The bed is kept flat as tolerated for turning; raising the head increases shearing and misaligns the spine.
distractorExplanations.d: A dependent resident needs assistance or a draw sheet; turning alone and fast risks injury to resident and NA.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-adls-safety-00.explanation: Logrolling/assistance protects skin and musculoskeletal injury. Follow the care plan for the number of staff and devices needed.

options.a: Keep a resident safely seated in a wheelchair between activities
options.b: Lift a resident from the floor after a fall by pulling up on the belt
options.c: Provide a secure hold to assist ambulation/transfers when appropriate
options.d: Pull the resident up in bed by grasping the belt at the back

distractorExplanations.a: Using a gait belt to hold someone in a chair makes it a restraint; it is a transfer and walking aid.
distractorExplanations.b: A fallen resident is assessed by the nurse first and raised with a mechanical lift, not hauled up by a gait belt.
distractorExplanations.d: Moving a resident up in bed uses a lift or draw sheet; gait belts are for transfers and ambulation.

options.a: Positioning flat on the back and rinsing with a full cup of water
options.b: Positioning upright and having the resident swish mouthwash
options.c: Positioning on the side and holding the mouth open with your fingers during care
options.d: Positioning on the side, using swabs per protocol, and protecting the airway

distractorExplanations.a: Lying flat with liquid in the mouth risks aspiration; the unconscious resident is turned on the side.
distractorExplanations.b: An unconscious resident cannot swish or spit; this assumes a conscious resident and risks aspiration.
distractorExplanations.c: Fingers should not go into an unconscious resident's mouth; a padded tongue blade is used to keep it open.

options.a: Put the weaker arm into clothing first and remove it last
options.b: Put the stronger arm into clothing first and remove it last
options.c: Put the weaker arm into clothing last and remove it first
options.d: Put both arms in at once while the resident leans forward

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the rule: the strong side goes in last and comes out first so the weak arm is not forced.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses both steps; the weak arm is dressed first and undressed last to minimize its movement.
distractorExplanations.d: Threading both arms together forces the weak limb; dress the weak side first, one arm at a time.

options.a: Massage reddened bony areas firmly to restore blood flow
options.b: Reposition immobile residents at least every 2 hours and keep skin clean/dry
options.c: Reposition immobile residents every 4 hours and use extra layers of padding under them
options.d: Keep the head of the bed raised above 30° to improve breathing at all times

distractorExplanations.a: Massaging reddened skin over bony prominences damages tissue further; report the redness instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Every 4 hours is too long, and extra linen layers trap heat and moisture; reposition at least every 2 hours.
distractorExplanations.d: Raising the head above 30° increases sacral shearing; keep it as low as the resident's condition allows.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-adls-safety-00.explanation: Pressure relief and moisture control are core prevention strategies. The care plan may set a different turning schedule.

options.a: Pull the resident up by the arms with the head of the bed raised
options.b: Have the resident push with heels while one NA drags the shoulders
options.c: Use proper lift/assist techniques and enough help; avoid dragging the skin
options.d: Raise the knee gatch high so the resident stops sliding, and leave them in that spot

distractorExplanations.a: Pulling under the arms with the bed raised causes shearing and shoulder injury; lower the head and use a lift sheet.
distractorExplanations.b: Dragging shears the skin; a dependent resident needs a lift sheet and two staff members.
distractorExplanations.d: Raising the knees does not correct the slide; the resident must first be moved up with a lift sheet and help.

options.a: From back to front for females, using clean areas of the washcloth
options.b: From front to back for females, reusing the same area of the washcloth
options.c: From the anal area upward first, then the labia, with one wipe
options.d: From front to back for females, using clean areas of the washcloth

distractorExplanations.a: Back to front carries bacteria from the anal area to the urethra and raises urinary tract infection risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Reusing the same area of the cloth spreads microorganisms; a clean part is used for each stroke.
distractorExplanations.c: Cleaning the anal area first and moving upward contaminates the urethral area; clean from front to back.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-adls-safety-00.explanation: Front-to-back reduces UTI risk; standard precautions and privacy apply. Privacy and dignity are maintained throughout.

options.a: Control the fall and lower the resident gently to the floor
options.b: Catch the resident under the arms and hold them upright
options.c: Hold the resident upright and walk quickly to the nearest chair
options.d: Lower the resident to the floor, then help them stand right away

distractorExplanations.b: Trying to stop a fall by holding a resident upright often injures both; ease them down to the floor instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Rushing a falling resident to a chair risks a worse fall; guide them gently to the floor.
distractorExplanations.d: After a fall the resident stays down until the nurse checks for injury; do not get them up immediately.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-adls-safety-00.explanation: Safe fall techniques reduce injury to resident and NA; then assess and report. Protect the head, then call for help; do not get the resident up before the nurse assesses.

options.a: Performed past the point of pain to increase joint flexibility
options.b: Performed as ordered, supporting joints, stopping if pain occurs
options.c: Performed quickly with each joint moved 20 times per session
options.d: Performed on the neck for every resident to prevent contractures

distractorExplanations.a: Range of motion stops at the point of pain or resistance; forcing it can injure the joint.
distractorExplanations.c: ROM is done slowly and smoothly with a few repetitions per joint as ordered, not fast high counts.
distractorExplanations.d: Neck ROM is done only when ordered and is often limited to licensed or therapy staff, not routine for everyone.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-adls-safety-01.explanation: ROM preserves mobility; never force through pain; follow care plan. Report any changes to the nurse.

options.a: Remove the top linens fully so the bottom sheet is easier to reach
options.b: Have the resident sit in a chair while you change the occupied bed
options.c: Keep the resident covered and roll them toward the open side without rails
options.d: Keep the resident covered for privacy/warmth and use side rails per policy

distractorExplanations.a: Leaving the resident uncovered violates privacy and warmth; a bath blanket keeps them covered.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes making an unoccupied bed; an occupied bed is made with the resident in it.
distractorExplanations.c: Rolling toward an unprotected side risks a fall; roll toward a raised rail or a second staff member.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-adls-safety-01.explanation: Occupied bedmaking maintains safety, dignity, and infection control. A raised rail or second staff member on the far side keeps the resident safe during turning.

options.a: Promote independence for residents with limited grip or coordination
options.b: Replace hand-feeding for residents with dysphagia and aspiration risk
options.c: Speed up meals so residents finish within the scheduled meal time
options.d: Reduce portion sizes for residents on calorie-restricted diets

distractorExplanations.b: Built-up utensils help grip, not swallowing; dysphagia needs diet texture changes and supervision.
distractorExplanations.c: Adaptive devices aim at independence and dignity, not faster meals for staff scheduling.
distractorExplanations.d: Portion control is a dietary order; adaptive utensils address limits in grip and coordination.

options.a: Check water temperature with the resident's foot before they step in
options.b: Check water temperature (safely warm) and ensure grab bars/nonslip surfaces
options.c: Check that the resident can lock the door for privacy during the shower
options.d: Set the water as hot as the resident prefers, then step out to give privacy

distractorExplanations.a: The NA checks water with a thermometer or the inner wrist; residents may have impaired sensation in the feet.
distractorExplanations.c: A locked door prevents help in an emergency; privacy is protected with curtains and covering instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Water must be safely warm per policy, and an at-risk resident should not be left alone in the shower.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-adls-safety-01.explanation: Burns and falls are major shower risks. Stay within safety guidelines and do not leave an at-risk resident alone.

options.a: On clean dry legs, rolled down tightly at the top to stay in place
options.b: After the resident has been up walking for an hour, so the legs are warm and relaxed
options.c: On clean dry legs, without wrinkles, as ordered—usually in the morning
options.d: At bedtime and left on overnight so legs rest compressed

distractorExplanations.a: Rolling the top creates a tourniquet effect; stockings must lie smooth without wrinkles or rolls.
distractorExplanations.b: Stockings go on before the resident gets up, while leg swelling is lowest, not after walking.
distractorExplanations.d: They are applied in the morning before getting up and removed as ordered for skin checks, not started at bedtime.

options.a: Use hand hygiene and appropriate PPE for all residents as indicated
options.b: Use gloves and gowns only for residents with a known infection
options.c: Use hand hygiene only when hands are visibly soiled after care
options.d: Use an N95 respirator and gown when entering every resident's room during care

distractorExplanations.b: Standard precautions apply to every resident regardless of diagnosis, not just those with known infections.
distractorExplanations.c: Hand hygiene is required before and after each contact; alcohol rub is used when hands are not visibly soiled.
distractorExplanations.d: N95 respirators are for airborne precautions such as TB; standard precautions match PPE to the expected exposure.

distractorExplanations.a: 93–95°F is in the hypothermic range, well below a normal oral temperature.
distractorExplanations.b: That range is the typical normal axillary temperature, about 1°F lower than an oral reading.
distractorExplanations.d: 98.6–100.6°F is the normal rectal range, about 1°F higher than an oral reading.

options.a: Tell the resident to breathe normally while you count their breaths
options.b: Count for 15 seconds and multiply by 2 to get the rate per minute
options.c: Count each inhalation and exhalation as two separate breaths
options.d: Count without telling the resident you are counting breaths

distractorExplanations.a: Announcing the count makes residents change their breathing; count without telling them.
distractorExplanations.b: A 15-second count is multiplied by 4, and irregular breathing needs a full 60-second count.
distractorExplanations.c: One rise and fall of the chest (inhale plus exhale) counts as one respiration, not two.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-infection-vita.explanation: Awareness alters breathing; observe rise/fall for 30–60 seconds per policy. Count right after the pulse and note rate and effort.

options.a: Wrist on the thumb side
options.b: Wrist on the little-finger side
options.c: Inner elbow (antecubital area)
options.d: Side of the neck below the jaw

distractorExplanations.b: The radial artery is on the thumb side; the little-finger side is the ulnar artery.
distractorExplanations.c: The inner elbow is the brachial pulse site used for blood pressure, not the radial pulse.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the carotid pulse, used in emergencies such as CPR, not the radial pulse.

options.a: Wear an N95 respirator and keep the door closed in a negative-pressure room
options.b: Wear gloves and a gown only, since droplets spread by touching surfaces
options.c: Wear a mask when working within close range of the resident as directed
options.d: Wear a mask when the resident is coughing, and skip it otherwise

distractorExplanations.a: N95 respirators and negative-pressure rooms are airborne precautions (TB, measles), not droplet precautions.
distractorExplanations.b: Gloves and gown alone are contact precautions; droplet precautions add a mask for close contact.
distractorExplanations.d: Droplet precautions call for a mask whenever working close to the resident, not just during coughing.

options.a: Carried against the uniform and placed in the bag at the end of care
options.b: Shaken out gently over the bed to remove crumbs and debris, then bagged promptly
options.c: Placed on the floor near the door until the hamper is brought in
options.d: Held away from the uniform and placed in appropriate bags; never shaken

distractorExplanations.a: Holding linen against the uniform transfers microorganisms to clothing; hold it away from your body.
distractorExplanations.b: Shaking linen spreads microorganisms into the air; roll it inward instead.
distractorExplanations.c: The floor is considered dirty; linen placed there contaminates the room and the hamper.

options.a: Nail polish, poor perfusion, or motion interferes with the sensor
options.b: The resident's blood pressure is mildly elevated during the reading
options.c: The sensor is placed on a warm, still finger without nail polish
options.d: The resident has eaten a meal shortly before the reading is taken

distractorExplanations.b: Mild hypertension does not distort SpO2; poor perfusion from cold hands or low blood pressure does.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes ideal placement, which gives an accurate reading rather than a distorted one.
distractorExplanations.d: Eating does not affect pulse oximetry; meal timing matters for blood glucose, not oxygen saturation.

options.a: Zero the scale and weigh at any time of day that suits the schedule
options.b: Balance/zero the scale, use consistent clothing/footwear approach
options.c: Have the resident wear shoes and a robe for warmth and safety
options.d: Ask the resident for their usual weight and record it if close

distractorExplanations.a: Weights are taken at the same time of day (often before breakfast) so readings can be compared.
distractorExplanations.c: Consistent minimal clothing without shoes is standard; shoes and robes inflate and vary the weight.
distractorExplanations.d: Self-reported weight is not a measurement; the NA must weigh the resident on a balanced scale.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-infection-vita.explanation: Accurate weights guide clinical decisions (heart failure, nutrition) Assist the resident for safety getting on and off the scale.

options.a: Remove the mask first so you can breathe freely while removing the rest
options.b: Remove gloves last so your hands stay protected throughout
options.c: Remove items in any order, then wash hands once at the end
options.d: Remove the most contaminated items first in the order taught

distractorExplanations.a: The mask or respirator comes off last; gloves, the most contaminated item, come off first.
distractorExplanations.b: Gloves are the most contaminated item and are removed first; keeping them on spreads contamination.
distractorExplanations.c: Order matters to prevent self-contamination; doffing follows a set sequence, then hand hygiene.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-infection-vita.explanation: Correct doffing prevents self-contamination. Finish with hand hygiene.

options.a: Too low (bradypnea)—report promptly
options.b: Normal for an adult at rest
options.c: Too high (tachypnea)—report promptly
options.d: Low but expected during sleep—no report

distractorExplanations.b: Normal adult respirations are about 12–20 per minute; 8 is below that range.
distractorExplanations.c: Tachypnea means a rate above about 20 per minute; 8 breaths/min is abnormally slow.
distractorExplanations.d: A rate of 8 is below the normal 12–20 range even at rest and must be reported, not dismissed.

options.a: Cleaning the tubing toward the meatus, keeping the bag on the bed rail
options.b: Cleaning the peri area and catheter tubing, keeping the bag below bladder level
options.c: Cleaning the peri area, then disconnecting the tubing to empty the bag
options.d: Cleaning the peri area and catheter tubing, resting the bag on the floor below the bed

distractorExplanations.a: Tubing is cleaned away from the meatus, and the bag hangs on the bed frame, not a movable rail.
distractorExplanations.c: The closed drainage system must stay connected; the bag is emptied through its drain spout.
distractorExplanations.d: The bag must not touch the floor, which contaminates the drain spout; hang it below bladder level on the frame.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-infection-vita.explanation: Closed system and dependent drainage reduce UTI risk. Cleaning follows the care plan, and the catheter is secured to prevent pulling.

options.a: Use it if the wrapper still looks dry and intact on inspection
options.b: Move it to a clean area and continue with the dressing change
options.c: Consider it contaminated and obtain new supplies per procedure
options.d: Cover it with a clean towel and use it within 30 minutes

distractorExplanations.a: An unattended sterile field is considered contaminated even if it looks intact; sterility cannot be verified.
distractorExplanations.b: Moving it does not restore sterility; once left unattended in a dirty area it must be replaced.
distractorExplanations.d: Covering a contaminated field does not make it sterile again; obtain new supplies.

options.a: Listening, clarifying, and allowing time for the resident to express feelings
options.b: Reassuring the resident quickly that everything will be fine
options.c: Giving advice on what the resident should do to solve the problem right away
options.d: Asking 'why' questions so the resident explains the reasons for their behavior

distractorExplanations.b: False reassurance shuts down feelings; it is a classic barrier to therapeutic communication.
distractorExplanations.c: Giving personal advice is a nontherapeutic block; the NA listens and lets the resident express feelings.
distractorExplanations.d: 'Why' questions can feel judgmental and make residents defensive; open-ended questions work better.

options.a: Remind her gently each time that her husband has died so she stays oriented
options.b: Respond with empathy and use redirection/validation techniques per care plan
options.c: Tell her he is on his way so she will stop asking
options.d: Ask the nurse for a sedative to calm her down quickly whenever she asks

distractorExplanations.a: Repeatedly reorienting to a death makes her relive the grief; validation and redirection are preferred in dementia.
distractorExplanations.c: False promises can raise agitation when he does not arrive; validate her feelings and redirect instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Medication is not a first response to a question; nonpharmacologic validation and redirection come first.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-psychosocial-0.explanation: Validation/redirection can reduce distress; follow the care plan and nurse guidance. Repeated harsh corrections only renew her grief.

options.a: Treat all residents the same way to avoid any appearance of bias
options.b: Use a resident's family members as interpreters for medical and care issues
options.c: Respect preferences about food, touch, privacy, and end-of-life customs
options.d: Assume residents from the same culture share the same preferences

distractorExplanations.a: Identical treatment ignores cultural differences; sensitivity means adapting care to individual preferences.
distractorExplanations.b: Facilities should use trained interpreters; family interpreting risks errors and privacy problems.
distractorExplanations.d: That is stereotyping; each resident's own preferences must be asked about and respected.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-psychosocial-0.explanation: Person-centered care includes cultural humility. This is done within facility rules.

options.a: Tell the resident things will look better tomorrow and leave
options.b: Distract the resident right away with a TV program or activity
options.c: Call the family member back to find out what upset the resident
options.d: Sit with the resident, offer presence, and ask if they want to talk

distractorExplanations.a: False reassurance followed by leaving dismisses feelings; offering presence and listening is supportive.
distractorExplanations.b: Immediate distraction avoids the feelings; first acknowledge them and offer to listen.
distractorExplanations.c: Contacting the caller breaches privacy and the NA role; support the resident and involve the nurse if needed.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-psychosocial-0.explanation: Emotional support and confidentiality are part of psychosocial care. Offer to have the nurse notified if needed.

options.a: Respected as a normal human need within consent, privacy, and safety policies
options.b: Discouraged because it is unsafe for most residents in their age group
options.c: Reported to the family each time a resident shows romantic interest
options.d: Allowed only between residents who were married before admission

distractorExplanations.b: Older adults keep sexual needs; blanket discouragement is ageist and violates resident rights.
distractorExplanations.c: Consenting relationships are private; reporting them to family breaches confidentiality and dignity.
distractorExplanations.d: Consenting adult residents may form new relationships; prior marriage is not a requirement.

options.a: Speak loudly into the better ear while standing slightly behind the resident
options.b: Face the resident, speak clearly at a moderate pace, and reduce background noise
options.c: Speak slowly with exaggerated lip movements and a raised pitch
options.d: Remove hearing aids during conversation so whistling feedback does not distract them

distractorExplanations.a: Standing behind removes lip-reading cues, and shouting distorts sound; face the resident instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Exaggerated mouthing distorts lip-reading and high pitches are harder to hear; use a normal, lower tone.
distractorExplanations.d: Hearing aids should be in place and working; removing them makes communication harder.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-psychosocial-0.explanation: Communication adaptations reduce isolation. Use assistive devices such as hearing aids.

options.a: Guides the resident by holding their arm and pushing them forward
options.b: Moves furniture to new spots to create wider walking paths
options.c: Identifies self when entering and explains care before touching
options.d: Speaks louder than usual so the resident knows where the NA is

distractorExplanations.a: The resident holds the NA's arm and walks slightly behind; pushing them forward is unsafe.
distractorExplanations.b: Rearranging furniture disorients residents with vision loss; keep items in familiar places.
distractorExplanations.d: Vision loss does not call for louder speech; identifying yourself on entry is what orients the resident.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-psychosocial-0.explanation: Consistency and verbal cueing support independence and safety. Keep pathways clear and furniture in familiar places.

options.a: Stages of grief that residents move through after a major loss
options.b: Sensory losses that affect hearing, vision, and the sense of touch in older adults
options.c: Swallowing problems that affect chewing, eating, and fluid intake
options.d: Neurologic changes that affect recognition, language, and skilled movement

distractorExplanations.a: Grief stages (Kübler-Ross) are denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance, not these terms.
distractorExplanations.b: These terms describe cognitive/neurologic deficits, not primary hearing, vision, or touch losses.
distractorExplanations.c: Swallowing difficulty is dysphagia; aphasia is a language deficit, not a swallowing problem.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-psychosocial-0.explanation: Understanding cognitive/communication deficits improves care and reduces agitation. These changes call for patience and adapted communication.

options.a: Listen respectfully and involve the nurse/supervisor
options.b: Explain the resident's diagnosis to calm the family down
options.c: Agree that the other staff are at fault to ease tension
options.d: Ask the family to write a letter to the state agency first

distractorExplanations.b: Explaining diagnoses is outside the NA role; the nurse handles clinical questions.
distractorExplanations.c: Blaming coworkers is unprofessional; listen and report concerns through the chain of command.
distractorExplanations.d: Families may complain to the state, but the NA's first step is to listen and involve the supervisor.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-psychosocial-0.explanation: Service recovery and escalation maintain trust; stay in scope. Concerns beyond the NA role go to the nurse or supervisor.

options.a: Scheduling every resident into the same group activities each day
options.b: Encouraging appropriate social activities and meaningful conversation
options.c: Moving the resident to a private room to reduce noise and distraction
options.d: Keeping the TV on in the room so the resident hears voices all day

distractorExplanations.a: Mandatory identical group activities ignore preferences; meaningful engagement is person-centered.
distractorExplanations.c: Isolation in a private room can deepen loneliness; social contact is what reduces it.
distractorExplanations.d: Background TV is not meaningful interaction and may ignore preferences; real conversation reduces loneliness.

options.a: Explain the bath is required by the care plan and proceed gently but firmly
options.b: Skip the bath and chart that it was completed to avoid conflict
options.c: Ask about concerns, offer choices (time/type), and report refusal per policy
options.d: Have the family call and persuade the resident to take the bath as scheduled

distractorExplanations.a: Residents have the right to refuse care; proceeding after a refusal violates resident rights.
distractorExplanations.b: Charting care that was not given is falsification; refusals must be documented and reported.
distractorExplanations.d: The first step is the NA's own inquiry and offer of choices; calling family is not the initial response.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-psychosocial-0.explanation: Consent and dignity apply; negotiate and escalate to the nurse. Never force a resident to bathe.

options.a: Restores short-term memory loss caused by Alzheimer's disease
options.b: Keeps residents focused on present-day facts like the date, time, and place
options.c: Replaces the need for structured activities and social programs
options.d: Supports identity, mood, and cognitive engagement for many older adults

distractorExplanations.a: Reminiscence draws on intact long-term memories; it does not reverse short-term memory loss.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes reality orientation, a different technique from reminiscence.
distractorExplanations.c: Reminiscence is one activity among many; it does not replace a full activity program.

options.a: Set a clear respectful boundary and report per policy
options.b: Laugh it off to keep the relationship friendly and avoid conflict
options.c: Request a reassignment without telling the resident or the nurse
options.d: Report it only if the comment is repeated during the same shift

distractorExplanations.b: Laughing it off signals acceptance and lets the behavior continue; set a boundary and report it.
distractorExplanations.c: Avoidance without reporting leaves the behavior unaddressed; the nurse must be informed.
distractorExplanations.d: Even a single inappropriate comment is addressed and reported per policy, not just repeated ones.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-psychosocial-0.explanation: Protect yourself and maintain professionalism; facilities have reporting pathways. State calmly that the behavior is inappropriate.

options.a: Following the facility's standard schedule so care is consistent for every resident
options.b: Knowing the resident’s preferences, routines, and life story to guide daily care
options.c: Letting the family make daily care choices for the resident
options.d: Focusing care on the resident's diagnosis and medical treatment plan

distractorExplanations.a: Uniform facility schedules are task-centered; person-centered care adapts to individual routines.
distractorExplanations.c: Residents make their own choices when able; family input supports but does not replace them.
distractorExplanations.d: That is a medical/task model; person-centered care centers the whole person and their preferences.

options.a: Gives a detailed medical explanation of every risk of the procedure
options.b: Tells the resident there is nothing to worry about and moves on
options.c: Explains what will happen in simple terms and stays calm and supportive
options.d: Waits until the procedure starts to explain so the resident worries less

distractorExplanations.a: Detailed risk explanations are the nurse's or provider's role and can increase anxiety.
distractorExplanations.b: False reassurance dismisses fears; simple explanations and calm support reduce anxiety.
distractorExplanations.d: Explaining before care starts, not during it, lets the resident prepare and lowers anxiety.

options.a: Giving medications and sterile invasive procedures not delegated legally
options.b: Measuring and recording intake and output as assigned
options.c: Collecting routine urine and stool specimens as directed by the nurse
options.d: Applying non-prescription moisturizing lotion to intact skin during routine care

distractorExplanations.b: Intake and output measurement is a routine NA task within scope, not outside it.
distractorExplanations.c: Routine specimen collection is within the NA's scope when assigned by the nurse.
distractorExplanations.d: Applying non-medicated lotion to intact skin is standard NA care, not a medication task.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-role-rights-00.explanation: NAs do not practice nursing/medicine beyond training and legal delegation. Some states allow specially trained medication aides to give certain medications.

options.a: Attempt the task carefully and report afterward how it went
options.b: Refuse politely and explain, then notify the nurse/supervisor
options.c: Ask an experienced NA to talk you through it as you do it
options.d: Complete it if the resident gives verbal consent to proceed

distractorExplanations.a: Doing an untrained task risks harm even if reported later; refuse and notify the nurse first.
distractorExplanations.c: Coaching from another NA does not bring the task within your training or scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Resident consent does not expand the NA's scope of practice or training.

options.a: Privacy, dignity, freedom from abuse, and staff-chosen daily schedules for safety
options.b: Dignity, privacy, freedom from restraints, and mail opened by staff for safety checks
options.c: Privacy, dignity, freedom from abuse/restraints, and participation in care decisions
options.d: Privacy and dignity, freedom from abuse, with care decisions made by the facility

distractorExplanations.a: Residents choose their own schedules where possible; staff-chosen routines conflict with self-determination.
distractorExplanations.b: Residents have the right to send and receive private, unopened mail.
distractorExplanations.d: Residents participate in care planning; decisions are not made for them by the facility.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-role-rights-00.explanation: OBRA and facility policies protect resident rights in nursing homes. Restraints may be used only with proper orders.

options.a: Threatening to withhold a resident's meal if they do not cooperate
options.b: Taking money from a resident's drawer without permission
options.c: Restraining a resident to a chair without a provider's order
options.d: Failing to provide needed care such as turning, fluids, or hygiene

distractorExplanations.a: Threats are verbal/psychological abuse, not neglect, which is a failure to provide needed care.
distractorExplanations.b: That is misappropriation of resident property, not neglect.
distractorExplanations.c: An unordered restraint is physical abuse or involuntary seclusion, not neglect.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-role-rights-00.explanation: Neglect is failure to provide goods/services necessary to avoid harm. Neglect creates a risk of harm.

options.a: Report immediately through the required chain/hotline per facility and state law
options.b: Gather more evidence over a few days before reporting it to the charge nurse
options.c: Confront the suspected staff member privately first, before telling anyone else about it
options.d: Report it only if the resident confirms the abuse happened

distractorExplanations.b: Suspected abuse must be reported immediately; delaying to gather proof is not allowed.
distractorExplanations.c: Confronting the person can endanger the resident and the evidence; report through the required channel.
distractorExplanations.d: Suspicion alone requires a report; residents may be unable or afraid to confirm.

options.a: Sharing resident information with any family member who calls
options.b: Sharing resident information only with those who need it to provide care
options.c: Discussing residents only with coworkers in break rooms or elevators
options.d: Keeping resident information from the nurse unless the resident agrees

distractorExplanations.a: Family access depends on the resident's permission; an unverified caller cannot receive information.
distractorExplanations.c: Public areas like elevators and break rooms are not appropriate places to discuss residents.
distractorExplanations.d: Care team members who need information for care can receive it; withholding it from the nurse harms care.

options.a: Requested by the family to keep a wandering resident safe
options.b: Applied by staff in an emergency and left in place until the next shift
options.c: Ordered by a provider, used as a last resort with least restriction
options.d: Ordered by a provider and checked once per shift for circulation

distractorExplanations.a: Family requests do not authorize restraints; a provider order and less restrictive alternatives come first.
distractorExplanations.b: Emergency use requires a prompt order and close monitoring; leaving it until the next shift is unsafe.
distractorExplanations.d: Restrained residents are checked often (e.g., every 15 minutes) and released at least every 2 hours, not once a shift.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-role-rights-00.explanation: Improper restraint use is abuse; know release/check requirements. Restraints must also be monitored per policy.

options.a: Completed at the end of the shift from memory to save time
options.b: Written before care is given so the record is ready on time
options.c: Corrected by erasing errors neatly so the record looks clean
options.d: Objective, timely, legible, and free of opinions/blame language

distractorExplanations.a: Documentation is done promptly after care, not reconstructed from memory at shift end.
distractorExplanations.b: Charting care before it is done is falsification; document only after the care is given.
distractorExplanations.c: Errors are corrected with a single line, date and initials (or per EHR policy), not by erasing.

nnaap-cna-readiness-check-role-rights-00.explanation: If it wasn’t documented, it is hard to prove it was done—never fabricate. Electronic entries must follow the same standards.

options.a: Answered promptly and placed within the resident’s reach
options.b: Answered promptly and stored out of reach while sleeping
options.c: Answered by the resident's assigned NA only
options.d: Placed within reach during the day shift

distractorExplanations.b: The call light must stay within reach at all times, including while the resident sleeps.
distractorExplanations.c: Any staff member who sees a call light should answer it, not just the assigned NA.
distractorExplanations.d: The call light must be within reach on every shift, not just during the day.

options.a: A facility employee who supervises nursing assistant staffing
options.b: An advocate who helps residents with complaints and rights issues
options.c: A state surveyor who inspects facilities and issues citations
options.d: A court-appointed guardian who makes decisions for residents

distractorExplanations.a: That describes a staffing coordinator or DON; the ombudsman is an independent resident advocate.
distractorExplanations.c: State surveyors inspect and cite; the ombudsman advocates for residents and resolves complaints.
distractorExplanations.d: Guardians make legal decisions for incapacitated residents; ombudsmen advocate but do not decide.

options.a: Are covered only when they work directly with electronic records
options.b: Are allowed to share PHI with any staff member in the facility
options.c: Handle PHI daily and can cause breaches through talk, records, or devices
options.d: Must get written consent before telling the nurse about a resident's condition

distractorExplanations.a: HIPAA covers PHI in every form, including spoken and paper information, not just electronic records.
distractorExplanations.b: PHI is shared with staff who need it for care (minimum necessary), not with any employee.
distractorExplanations.d: Sharing information with the care team for treatment does not require written consent.

options.a: Accept the money and give it to the nurse to hold for the unit
options.b: Accept if the amount is small and the resident insists firmly
options.c: Accept and record the gift in the resident's chart for honesty
options.d: Politely refuse gifts of money per policy and thank them verbally

distractorExplanations.a: Accepting the gift at all violates policy; the NA should politely refuse it.
distractorExplanations.b: Small amounts are still prohibited cash gifts; the resident's insistence does not change policy.
distractorExplanations.c: Documenting a prohibited gift does not make it acceptable; refuse it politely instead.

options.a: Report problems to the appropriate supervisor so issues are addressed safely
options.b: Report problems directly to the administrator to get faster action on them
options.c: Decide which coworker should handle each resident's daily tasks
options.d: Report problems to the resident's family first, before the nurse knows about them

distractorExplanations.b: Skipping levels bypasses the chain of command; start with the immediate supervisor (the nurse).
distractorExplanations.c: Assignments come from the nurse; the chain of command is for reporting concerns upward.
distractorExplanations.d: Problems go first to the supervising nurse; the family is informed through proper channels.

options.a: Takes a scheduled meal break after giving report to a coworker on the unit
options.b: Leaves an assigned shift/residents without giving report or being relieved
options.c: Refuses an extra shift after completing the assigned one and giving report
options.d: Calls in sick before the shift following facility procedure

distractorExplanations.a: A scheduled break after handoff is not abandonment because the residents' care is covered.
distractorExplanations.c: Declining overtime after finishing the shift and reporting off is not abandonment.
distractorExplanations.d: Calling in before the shift per policy is not abandonment; leaving residents mid-shift without relief is.

options.a: “Resident seemed upset at lunch and probably vomited because she disliked the food.”
options.b: “Resident complained of feeling sick, looked uncomfortable, and ate poorly at lunch.”
options.c: “Resident ate 50% of lunch; stated abdominal pain 6/10; vomited 100 mL green fluid.”
options.d: “Resident is depressed and refused most of lunch as usual.”

distractorExplanations.a: 'Seemed' and 'probably' are interpretations and guesses about cause, not measurable observations.
distractorExplanations.b: 'Looked uncomfortable' and 'ate poorly' are vague impressions; objective notes record amounts and findings.
distractorExplanations.d: 'Depressed' is a diagnosis the NA cannot make, and 'as usual' is an opinion, not an observation.
